content:
Dear all,

we are happy to share the first public alpha of Lean Beam:

https://github.com/ejgallego/lean-beam

Install instructions and documentation are available there.

Lean Beam is an experimental project for making Lean more convenient to use from AI-assisted and tool-assisted workflows. It extends Lean’s LSP server with a small number of additional operations, and provides a lightweight broker exposing them through a CLI and an MCP server.

A central feature of Beam is speculative execution. With the runAt method, clients can try Lean commands or tactics at specific positions in saved files without changing those files. Because these probes can be issued concurrently, agents and tools can cheaply explore several “would this work here?” possibilities in the real module context.

Beam is intended to make that loop cheaper and more structured than repeatedly creating scratch files or using full lake build runs as the inner loop.

The current release also includes support for:

  • incrementally synchronizing Lean's view of a file after edits with the sync method;
  • inspecting existing code and proof state with hover, goals;
  • gathering actionable file information with todo, including sorries, holes, diagnostics, code actions, and incomplete proofs;
  • saving .olean artifacts from an interactive session with save.

We have found Beam useful for proof repair, proof search experiments, proof translation and porting, autoformalization experiments, and regular AI-assisted Lean editing.

Beam is implemented in Lean, which lets us integrate more directly with Lean in places where that matters, such as state ownership and synchronization.

The main goal of this public release is to gather feedback from Lean users and tool authors. We want to better understand what AI-assisted Lean workflows need in practice, and which capabilities would be most valuable for the Lean FRO to support officially in the future.

Beam itself remains experimental alpha-quality software. It is not yet a supported Lean FRO product, and we expect rough edges and interface changes as more people try it on real projects.

Feedback, issues, use cases, design comments, and contributions are very welcome.

Does lean-mcp-lsp depend on such scratch files?
Have you done any experiments on token savings? Even anecdotactly ?

Bas Spitters said:

Does lean-mcp-lsp depend on such scratch files?

If I’m not mistaken, lean-mcp-lsp uses “virtual” _mcp_scratch_* documents.

My reference to “scratch” files was mainly about a vanilla agent setup, where agents often create files under /tmp and then run lake build.

I think the main difference is parallelism: N concurrent probes require N scratch documents in lean-mcp-lsp, each with its own startup cost.

The trade-offs are subtle, especially with snapshot support now being added to Lean.

Have you done any experiments on token savings? Even anecdotactly ?

Not specifically for token usage, though I think that would be very useful to measure.

I did run some experiments on the computational savings from runAt while repairing proofs after a mathlib bump for Noperthedron. The results were quite good, with roughly a 50% reduction in Lean processing time.

Beam was originally an LSP extension designed to give agents and tools better access to live document state. Since agents generally did not use LSP directly, I added a simple CLI and later an MCP interface, which was fairly straightforward by that point.

I also looked at the trade-offs between CLI and MCP for Codex. My impression is that the distinction does not matter very much, since both ultimately compile down to the model’s primitive tool-call interface. Still, the trade-offs are subtle.

Until we have more usage data, I think we can only claim that Beam’s runAt method is asymptotically more efficient for speculative execution than the approaches that were previously available.

Doesn't lean-lsp-mcp have the multi-attempt tool for trying several things without editing the file? I think right now lean-lsp-mcp is the de-facto standard for AI assisted Lean coding. Which features of Beam should make the users of lean-lsp-mcp want to switch to Beam?

@Vasily Ilin

Thank you; this is a very important question, and I am working on making the distinction clearer in Beam's documentation.

lean-lsp-mcp has done an increbile job of demonstrating how much can be achieved through Lean’s existing LSP interface, including speculative evaluation through multi-attempt.

Beam explores a different design point: what additional capabilities and efficiency improvements become possible when we are willing to extend Lean’s server itself? Moreover, a key design point of Beam is that the source of truth about all Lean documents lives exclusively in the Lean LSP server, which greatly simplifies some design constraints and interaction patterns.

So far, I see three areas where closer Lean integration may be useful for users:

  • A better cost profile for speculative rechecking through runAt, potentially including asymptotic and parallelism improvements vs multi-attempt scratch file approach for workloads that explore many alternatives at different document positions.
  • More precise coordination of edits, synchronization, and readiness across multiple files than what is possible with vanilla LSP.
  • Richer file analysis using information that Lean already maintains internally but does not currently expose through standard LSP operations.

I'd recommend trying Beam if you have experienced issues with some of the areas above.

The broader goal for Beam is to reduce the cost of the agent's inner verification loop. These possibilities come from state, ownership, and lifecycle information already present inside Lean; Beam's role is to expose a small, agent-oriented interface to that information.

Beam's LSP extensions are not specific to Beam’s own CLI or MCP server. Other tools, including lean-lsp-mcp, can use them directly. It would be particularly valuable to see that integration happen: adoption by another tool would be strong evidence that an operation such as runAt is useful as a general Lean capability and may ultimately be worth upstreaming.

Historically, Beam began as a collection of Lean LSP extensions. Because those extensions were difficult to exercise and test directly, I added a thin CLI layer. The MCP server was added only recently as another thin interface over the same functionality, initially motivated largely by integration and conformance testing.

My original intention was to make the new extensions available through lean-lsp-mcp. I have not yet pursued that integration myself, primarily because I am not familiar with its Python codebase and have very limited Python experience.

At present, I view the projects as complementary. lean-lsp-mcp provides a broad and established interface for AI-assisted Lean development. Beam is intentionally focused on the narrower problem of improving execution, synchronization, analysis, and verification within the agent’s inner loop. There are currently no plans for Beam to reproduce the broader range of capabilities that lean-lsp-mcp already provides, such as theorem and premise search.

@Emilio Jesús Gallego Arias , do you have a side-by-side comparison of a specific benchmark or project, where Beam's advantages over lean-lsp-mcp are clearly demonstrated?

My experience with lean-lsp-mcp is that it's simply that thing that gives agents the same view that humans enjoy when working with Lean in VSCode (infoview, hover info, etc). I don't know what runAt is and what "richer file analysis" means, and I suspect that many others also don't know. But if you can show that giving claude code Beam instead of lean-lsp-mcp improves the time it takes to formalize X (project/benchmark) from M minutes to M' minutes with M'<M, this will be very convincing! Or if it improves token efficiency.
